## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can

be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Setting the authentication scheme¶ {#setting-the-authentication-scheme}

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`


You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.authenticationimportSessionAuthentication,BasicAuthenticationfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):authentication_classes=[SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication]permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`


Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.


`@api_view(['GET'])@authentication_classes([SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`


## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden

-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.

This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

Note that if deploying to

, the authorization header is not passed through to a WSGI application by default, as it is assumed that authentication will be handled by Apache, rather than at an application level.

If you are deploying to Apache, and using any non-session based authentication, you will need to explicitly configure mod_wsgi to pass the required headers through to the application.  This can be done by specifying the
`WSGIPassAuthorization`
directive in the appropriate context and setting it to
`'On'`

## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can
26| be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Setting the authentication scheme¶ {#setting-the-authentication-scheme}

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`


You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden
26|-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware. 
26| This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

If you are deploying to Apache, and using any non-session based authentication, you will need to explicitly configure mod_wsgi to pass the required headers through to the application.  This can be done by specifying the
`WSGIPassAuthorization`
directive in the appropriate context and setting it to

user_input: The OpenAPI file we publish is missing a good chunk of the API. None of the custom actions we hung off our viewsets appear in it at all, and several endpoints that do appear describe their request body as empty even though they clearly accept one. Nothing fails — the generate step exits cleanly and writes the file. What is actually walking the project to build this, where does the per-endpoint detail come from, and why would an endpoint come out blank rather than wrong?
reference: Schema generation is two layers, and your two symptoms come from different ones. SchemaGenerator is the top-level piece: it walks your configured URL patterns, finds the APIView subclasses behind them, asks each one for its schema representation, and compiles the result — so anything not reachable through the URL conf simply isn't seen, which is the first thing to check for the missing actions. The per-view detail comes from AutoSchema, which is attached to each view through its `schema` attribute and does the introspection; you subclass AutoSchema to customise what a view reports, and set a project-wide default with the DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS setting. An endpoint comes out blank rather than wrong when the introspection has nothing to infer from — there's no serializer for it to read — which is why the docs tell you to annotate the generated schema with any additional information that cannot be automatically inferred. Worth knowing before you invest in this: the built-in schema support is deprecated in favour of third-party packages, and drf-spectacular is the recommended full replacement.
reference_contexts: SchemaGenerator is a top-level class that is responsible for walking your configured URL patterns, finding APIView subclasses, enquiring for their schema representation, and compiling the final schema object.
AutoSchema encapsulates all the details necessary for per-view schema introspection. Is attached to each view via the schema attribute. You subclass AutoSchema in order to customize your schema.
settings.DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS allows you to specify an AutoSchema subclass to serve as your project's default.
Once you've generated a schema in this way you can annotate it with any additional information that cannot be automatically inferred by the schema generator.

REST framework's built-in support for generating OpenAPI schemas is deprecated in favor of 3rd party packages that can provide this functionality instead. As a full-fledged replacement, we recommend the drf-spectacular package.
llm_response:
The `SchemaGenerator` class is responsible for walking your project's routed URL patterns to identify `APIView` subclasses and compile the final OpenAPI schema.

### Where per-endpoint detail comes from
The schema generation process relies on the introspection of `GenericAPIView` attributes and methods. Specifically:
*   **`get_components()`**: This method (defined in `AutoSchema`) generates the OpenAPI components that describe request and response bodies by deriving their properties from the view's serializer.
*   **`get_operation()`**: This method generates the OpenAPI operation object that describes the endpoint, including path and query parameters.

### Why endpoints appear blank or missing
*   **Missing custom actions**: The `SchemaGenerator` identifies `APIView` subclasses by walking routed URL patterns. If your custom actions are defined using the `@action` decorator, they are intended to be routable. However, the automatic introspection of components and operation parameters relies on the attributes and methods of `GenericAPIView` (such as `get_serializer()`). If your custom actions do not properly expose the necessary metadata or if the `SchemaGenerator` cannot resolve the serializer context for those specific actions, they may not be included in the generated output.
*   **Blank request bodies**: The request body is derived from the serializer via `get_components()`. If an endpoint appears to have an empty request body despite accepting one, it is likely because the view is not correctly configured to provide a serializer that the `SchemaGenerator` can introspect for that specific method. The `SchemaGenerator` compiles the schema by calling `get_components()` and `get_operation()` for every view, path, and allowed method; if the serializer is not correctly associated with the view's method handler, the generator will fail to populate the request body component.

**Recommendation:**
The Django REST framework's built-in OpenAPI schema generation is deprecated. The documentation recommends using **drf-spectacular**, which is specifically designed to generate OpenAPI 3 schemas and provides more robust support for automatic and customizable schema generation.

The serializer redesign in 3.0 did not include any public API for modifying how ModelSerializer classes automatically generate a set of fields from a given mode class. We've now re-introduced an API for this, allowing you to create new ModelSerializer base classes that behave differently, such as using a different default style for relationships.

For more information, see the documentation on
customizing field mappings (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#customizing-field-mappings)

user_input: I'm weighing limiting a queryset vs permission classes vs the serializer to restrict access. What can each control, especially for list vs create?
reference: queryset/get_queryset limits which existing objects are visible globally; permission_classes do action/object-level checks but object-level only applies to retrieve/modify/delete; serializer_class restricts at instance level on input/output. Object-level checks don't run on create because get_object isn't called.
reference_contexts: REST framework offers three different methods to customize access restrictions on a case-by-case basis.
These apply in different scenarios and have different effects and limitations.
Because the get_object() method is not called, object level permissions from the has_object_permission() method are not applied when creating objects.
The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses GenericAPIView is to override the .get_queryset() method.
The ModelSerializer class provides a shortcut that lets you automatically create a Serializer class with fields that correspond to the Model fields.
llm_response:
To restrict access, you can use `queryset`, `permission_classes`, or the `serializer_class`. Their capabilities regarding list and create actions are as follows:

### **1. QuerySet / `get_queryset()`**
*   **Control:** Limits the general visibility of objects from the database. It defines the set of objects that can be listed, modified, or deleted.
*   **List:** Acts as a global filter. It is the primary mechanism to restrict which objects are returned in a list view.
*   **Create:** Does not apply to create actions.
*   **Note:** You can override `get_queryset()` to return different querysets based on the current action or request user.

### **2. Permission Classes / `get_permissions()`**
*   **Control:** Performs general permission checks based on the current action, request, and targeted object.
*   **List:** Applies global permission checks to the entire object type. It cannot perform object-level filtering for list views; you must filter the queryset separately.
*   **Create:** Applies global permission checks to the entire object type. Because `get_object()` is not called during creation, `has_object_permission()` is not applied. To restrict creation, you must implement the check in your serializer or override `perform_create()`.

### **3. Serializer Class / `get_serializer()`**
*   **Control:** Manages instance-level restrictions that apply to all objects on input and output.
*   **List:** Can apply object-level restrictions. However, a serializer should not raise `PermissionDenied` during a list action, or the entire list will fail to return.
*   **Create:** Can apply object-level restrictions.

### **Summary Table**

| Method | List Action | Create Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`queryset`** | Global (filters visibility) | No |
| **`permission_classes`** | Global (checks authorization) | Global (checks authorization) |
| **`serializer_class`** | Object-level* | Object-level |

*\*Note: Serializers should not raise `PermissionDenied` during list actions.*

For more complex requirements, the documentation notes that the **Django Rest Framework PSQ** package allows `permission_classes`, `serializer_class`, and `queryset` to be action-based and dependent on permission-based rules. Additionally, for object-level permissions, you may need to use `check_object_permissions(request, obj)` in custom views or use packages like `django-guardian` with `DjangoObjectPermissions`.

## Third party packages¶ {#third-party-packages}

### DRF - Access Policy¶ {#drf-access-policy}

The
Django REST - Access Policy (https://github.com/rsinger86/drf-access-policy)

### Composed Permissions¶ {#composed-permissions}

The
Composed Permissions (https://github.com/niwibe/djangorestframework-composed-permissions)

Django REST Framework API Key (https://florimondmanca.github.io/djangorestframework-api-key/)

Or you can set the metadata class individually for a view:

The REST framework package only includes a single metadata class implementation, named
`SimpleMetadata`
. If you want to use an alternative style you'll need to implement a custom metadata class.

## Overview of access restriction methods¶ {#overview-of-access-restriction-methods}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

Before running the main body of the view each permission in the list is checked.
If any permission check fails, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

The request was successfully authenticated, but permission was denied.
— An HTTP 403 Forbidden response will be returned.
The request was not successfully authenticated, and the highest priority authentication class
does not
use
`WWW-Authenticate`

before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

### DRF - Access Policy¶ {#drf-access-policy}

The
Django REST - Access Policy (https://github.com/rsinger86/drf-access-policy)

Composed Permissions (https://github.com/niwibe/djangorestframework-composed-permissions)

REST Condition (https://github.com/caxap/rest_condition)

The REST framework package only includes a single metadata class implementation, named
`SimpleMetadata`
. If you want to use an alternative style you'll need to implement a custom metadata class.

To build your snippets API with the requested functionality and automatic URL routing, you should wire together the following DRF components:

### 1. Serializer
Use a `HyperlinkedModelSerializer` (e.g., `SnippetSerializer`) to manage the translation of your `Snippet` model. To handle the owner, include an `owner` field defined as `serializers.ReadOnlyField(source="owner.username")`. Ensure you add `'owner'` to the `fields` list in the serializer's `Meta` class.

### 2. ViewSet
Use a `ModelViewSet` (e.g., `SnippetViewSet`) to handle the logic. This provides full CRUD operations.
*   **Permissions:** Set `permission_classes` to `[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly, IsOwnerOrReadOnly]`. This ensures that only authenticated users can create snippets, and only the owner can update or delete them, while unauthenticated users retain read-only access.
*   **Ownership:** Override the `perform_create` method to associate the snippet with the user making the request:
    ```python
    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
    ```

### 3. Router
To avoid hand-writing `urls.py` entries for every route, use a `DefaultRouter`. This automatically determines the URL configuration based on your `ViewSet`.

### How they fit together
In your `urls.py`, you register your `ViewSet` with the `DefaultRouter` instance:

```python
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from snippets import views

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register(r"snippets", views.SnippetViewSet, basename="snippet")

urlpatterns = [
    path("", include(router.urls)),
]
```

By registering the `SnippetViewSet` with the `DefaultRouter`, the framework automatically generates the necessary list and detail routes for your API.

user_input: Reversing URLs in a versioned API gives links pointing at the wrong version. How do reverse() and versioning interact, and what must I pass?
reference: DRF's reverse ties into the versioning scheme, so pass the current request as a keyword argument; reverse then applies the URL transformations for that request's version and returns a fully qualified URL from the request's host/port.
reference_contexts: The reverse function included by REST framework ties in with the versioning scheme.
reverse import reverse reverse ( 'bookings-list' , request = request ) The above function will apply any URL transformations appropriate to the request version.
Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.
llm_response:
The `reverse()` function integrates with the framework's versioning scheme to apply appropriate URL transformations based on the version requested in the incoming client request.

To ensure `reverse()` generates the correct versioned URL, you must pass the current `request` object as a keyword argument to the function:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('bookings-list', request=request)
```

When the `request` is provided:
*   If using `NamespaceVersioning`, the function will resolve the URL using the namespace corresponding to the request version (e.g., `'v1:bookings-list'`).
*   If using `QueryParameterVersioning`, the function will include the version as a query parameter in the generated URL (e.g., `/?version=1.0`).

If you are using hyperlinked serializers with a URL-based versioning scheme, you must also include the `request` as context to the serializer to ensure generated URLs include the appropriate versioning:

```python
serializer = BookingsSerializer(queryset, many=True, context={'request': request})
```

# Versioning¶ {#versioning}

Versioning an interface is just a "polite" way to kill deployed clients.
—
Roy Fielding (https://www.slideshare.net/evolve_conference/201308-fielding-evolve/31)
.

API versioning allows you to alter behavior between different clients. REST framework provides for a number of different versioning schemes.

Versioning is determined by the incoming client request, and may either be based on the request URL, or based on the request headers.

There are a number of valid approaches to approaching versioning.
Non-versioned systems can also be appropriate (https://www.infoq.com/articles/roy-fielding-on-versioning)
, particularly if you're engineering for very long-term systems with multiple clients outside of your control.

## Versioning with REST framework¶ {#versioning-with-rest-framework}

When API versioning is enabled, the
`request.version`
attribute will contain a string that corresponds to the version requested in the incoming client request.

By default, versioning is not enabled, and
`request.version`
will always return
`None`
.

# Versioning¶ {#versioning}

Versioning an interface is just a "polite" way to kill deployed clients.
—
Roy Fielding (https://www.slideshare.net/evolve_conference/201308-fielding-evolve/31)
.

API versioning allows you to alter behavior between different clients. REST framework provides for a number of different versioning schemes.

Versioning is determined by the incoming client request, and may either be based on the request URL, or based on the request headers.

There are a number of valid approaches to approaching versioning.
Non-versioned systems can also be appropriate (https://www.infoq.com/articles/roy-fielding-on-versioning)
, particularly if you're engineering for very long-term systems with multiple clients outside of your control.

## Versioning with REST framework¶ {#versioning-with-rest-framework}

When API versioning is enabled, the
`request.version`
attribute will contain a string that corresponds to the version requested in the incoming client request.


115|By default, versioning is not enabled, and
`request.version`
will always return
`None`
.

### Varying behavior based on the version¶ {#varying-behavior-based-on-the-version}

How you vary the API behavior is up to you, but one example you might typically want is to switch to a different serialization style in a newer version. For example:


`defget_serializer_class(self):ifself.request.version=='v1':returnAccountSerializerVersion1returnAccountSerializer`


### Reversing URLs for versioned APIs¶ {#reversing-urls-for-versioned-apis}

The
`reverse`
function included by REST framework ties in with the versioning scheme. You need to make sure to include the current
`request`
as a keyword argument, like so.


`fromrest_framework.reverseimportreverse
reverse('bookings-list',request=request)`


The above function will apply any URL transformations appropriate to the request version. For example:

If
`NamespaceVersioning`
was being used, and the API version was 'v1', then the URL lookup used would be
`'v1:bookings-list'`
, which might resolve to a URL like
`http://example.org/v1/bookings/`
.
If
`QueryParameterVersioning`
was being used, and the API version was
`1.0`
, then the returned URL might be something like
`http://example.org/bookings
115|/?version=1.0`

### Versioned APIs and hyperlinked serializers¶ {#versioned-apis-and-hyperlinked-serializers}

When using hyperlinked serialization styles together with a URL based versioning scheme make sure to include the request as context to the serializer.


`defget(self,request):queryset=Booking.objects.all()serializer=BookingsSerializer(queryset,many=True,context={'request':request})returnResponse({'all_bookings':serializer.data})`


Doing so will allow any returned URLs to include the appropriate versioning.

## Configuring the versioning scheme¶ {#configuring-the-versioning-scheme}

The versioning scheme is defined by the
`DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS`
settings key.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS':'rest_framework.versioning.NamespaceVersioning'}`


Unless it is explicitly set, the value for
`DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS`
will be
`None`
. In this case the
`request.version`
attribute will always return
`None`
.

You can also set the versioning scheme on an individual view. Typically you won't need to do this, as it makes more sense to have a single versioning scheme used globally. If you do need to do so, use the
`versioning_class`
attribute.


`classProfileList(APIView):versioning_class=versioning.QueryParameterVersioning`

reference: They're separate but sequential: authentication identifies the request and runs first (setting request.user/request.auth), then permissions use that to allow or deny. Set authentication_classes and permission_classes together — authentication alone never grants access.

llm_response:
To control the authentication scheme and permissions on an `APIView`, you define them as class attributes. These attributes allow you to override global defaults for that specific view.

### How they relate
Authentication and permissions are distinct mechanisms that work together to determine if a request should be granted access:
*   **Authentication** determines the identity of the user (e.g., `request.user` and `request.auth`).
*   **Permissions** use that identity to authorize or deny access to the view.
*   Permission checks are run at the very start of the view, typically using the authentication information provided by the authentication classes.

### How to set them on an `APIView`
You set both by defining the `authentication_classes` and `permission_classes` attributes as lists within your `APIView` subclass.

**Example implementation:**

```python
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework import authentication, permissions

class MyCustomView(APIView):
    # Define the authentication schemes allowed for this view
    authentication_classes = [authentication.TokenAuthentication]
    
    # Define the permission classes required for this view
    permission_classes = [permissions.IsAdminUser]

    def get(self, request, format=None):
        return Response({"message": "Access granted"})
```

### Key points:
*   **Overrides:** By setting these attributes on the class, you tell the view to ignore the global defaults defined in your `settings.py` file.
*   **Multiple classes:** Both attributes accept a list, allowing you to specify multiple authentication or permission classes.
*   **Function-based views:** If you are using the `@api_view` decorator instead of a class, you must use the corresponding decorators `@authentication_classes` and `@permission_classes` placed **after** (below) the `@api_view` decorator.

# Throttling¶ {#throttling}

HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm
Twitter API rate limiting response (https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/basics/rate-limiting)

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide

/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework

is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

Before running the main body of the view each throttle in the list is checked.
If any throttle check fails an
`exceptions.Throttled`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`

The rates used in
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day. The period must be specified after the
`/`
separator using
`s`
,
`m`
,
`h`
or
`d`
, respectively. For increased clarity, extended units such as
`second`
,
`minute`

`hour`

`day`
or even abbreviations like
`

# Throttling¶ {#throttling}

HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm
Twitter API rate limiting response (https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/basics/rate-limiting)

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide
43|/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework
43| is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

Before running the main body of the view each throttle in the list is checked.
If any throttle check fails an
`exceptions.Throttled`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

## Setting the throttling policy¶ {#setting-the-throttling-policy}

The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`
and

The rates used in
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day. The period must be specified after the
`/`
separator using
`s`
,
`m`
,
`h`
or
`d`
, respectively. For increased clarity, extended units such as
`second`
,
`minute`
,
`hour`
,
`day`
or even abbreviations like
`
43|sec`
,
`min`
,
`hr`
are allowed, as only the first character is relevant to identify the rate.

You can also set the throttling policy on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.throttlingimportUserRateThrottlefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):throttle_classes=[UserRateThrottle]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`

user_input: When I POST invalid data, where does the flow that turns a serializer error into a 400 actually come from — the serializer or the view?
reference: Both cooperate: the serializer's is_valid(raise_exception=True) raises ValidationError, the generic views use raise_exception=True, and DRF's default exception handler converts it to a 400.
reference_contexts: The .is_valid() method takes an optional raise_exception flag that will cause it to raise a serializers.ValidationError exception if there are validation errors.
is_valid ( raise_exception = True ) The generic views use the raise_exception=True flag, which means that you can override the style of validation error responses globally in your API.

llm_response:
The flow that turns a serializer error into a 400 response is handled by the REST framework's default exception handler, which automatically processes `ValidationError` exceptions.

The origin of the error depends on how the validation is triggered:

*   **The Serializer:** The `ValidationError` is raised within the serializer (or its components) when input data is in an incorrect format or fails to meet specified criteria. This occurs during the `to_internal_value` method, within individual field validators, or via custom validation logic (such as the `validate()` method).
*   **The View:** While the serializer generates the error, the view is responsible for triggering the exception-handling flow if you use the `raise_exception=True` flag when calling `serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`. When this flag is used, the serializer raises a `ValidationError` that the REST framework's default exception handler automatically catches and converts into an HTTP 400 Bad Request response.

If you do not use `raise_exception=True`, the view must manually handle the error response, typically by checking `serializer.errors` and returning a `Response` with `status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST`.

# Django REST framework 3.0¶ {#django-rest-framework-30}

The 3.0 release of Django REST framework is the result of almost four years of iteration and refinement. It comprehensively addresses some of the previous remaining design issues in serializers, fields and the generic views.

This release is incremental in nature. There
are
some breaking API changes, and upgrading
will
require you to read the release notes carefully, but the migration path should otherwise be relatively straightforward.

The difference in quality of the REST framework API and implementation should make writing, maintaining and debugging your application far easier.

`ModelSerializer`
class and the explicit
`Serializer`
class.
A new
`BaseSerializer`
class, making it easier to write serializers for alternative storage backends, or to completely customize your serialization and validation logic.
A cleaner fields API including new classes such as
`ListField`
and
`MultipleChoiceField`
.
Super simple default implementations (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/blob/main/rest_framework/mixins.py)
for the generic views.
Support for overriding how validation errors are handled by your API.
A metadata API that allows you to customize how
`OPTIONS`
requests are handled by your API.
A more compact

JSON output with unicode style encoding turned on by default.
Templated based HTML form rendering for serializers. This will be finalized as public API in the upcoming 3.1 release.

Significant new functionality continues to be planned for the 3.1 and 3.2 releases. These releases will correspond to the two
Kickstarter stretch goals (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/tomchristie/django-rest-framework-3)
- "Feature improvements" and "Admin interface". Further 3.x releases will present simple upgrades, without the same level of fundamental API changes necessary for the 3.0 release.

#### REST framework: Under the hood.¶ {#rest-framework-under-the-hood}

This talk from the
Django: Under the Hood (https://www.djangounderthehood.com/)
event in Amsterdam, Nov 2014, gives some good background context on the design decisions behind 3.0.

Below is an in-depth guide to the API changes and migration notes for 3.0.

## Request objects¶ {#request-objects}

#### The.dataand.query_paramsproperties.¶ {#the-data-and-query_params-properties}

The usage of
`request.DATA`
and
`request.FILES`
is now pending deprecation in favor of a single
`request.data`
attribute that contains
all
the parsed data.

Having separate attributes is reasonable for web applications that only ever parse url-encoded or multipart requests, but makes less sense for the

general-purpose request parsing that REST framework supports.

You may now pass all the request data to a serializer class in a single argument:


`# Do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.data)`


Instead of passing the files argument separately:


`# Don't do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.DATA,files=request.FILES)`


The usage of
`request.QUERY_PARAMS`
is now pending deprecation in favor of the lowercased
`request.query_params`
.

## Serializers¶ {#serializers}

#### Single-step object creation.¶ {#single-step-object-creation}

Previously the serializers used a two-step object creation, as follows:

Validating the data would create an object instance. This instance would be available as
`serializer.object`
.
Calling
`serializer.save()`
would then save the object instance to the database.

This style is in-line with how the
`ModelForm`
class works in Django, but is problematic for a number of reasons:

Some data, such as many-to-many relationships, cannot be added to the object instance until after it has been saved. This type of data needed to be hidden in some undocumented state on the object instance, or kept as state on the serializer instance so that it could be used when
`.save()`
is called.
Instantiating model instances directly means that you cannot use model manager classes for instance creation, e.g.
`ExampleModel.objects.create(...)`
. Manager classes are an excellent layer at which to enforce business logic and

Validating the data makes the cleaned data available as
`serializer.validated_data`
.
Calling
`serializer.save()`
then saves and returns the new object instance.

The resulting API changes are further detailed below.

and

`.restore_object()`

and

and save

#### Usingserializers.ValidationError.¶ {#using-serializersvalidationerror}

Previously
`serializers.ValidationError`
error was simply a synonym for
`django.core.exceptions.ValidationError`

`APIException`
base class.

The reason behind this is that Django's
`ValidationError`
class is intended for use with HTML forms and its API makes using it slightly awkward with nested validation errors that can occur in serializers.

For most users this change shouldn't require any updates to your codebase, but it is worth ensuring

that whenever raising validation errors you should prefer using the
`serializers.ValidationError`
exception class, and not Django's built-in exception.

We strongly recommend that you use the namespaced import style of
`import serializers`

`from serializers import ValidationError`

#### Writable nested serialization.¶ {#writable-nested-serialization}

REST framework 2.x attempted to automatically support writable nested serialization, but the behavior was complex and non-obvious. Attempting to automatically handle these case is problematic:

There can be complex dependencies involved in order of saving multiple related model instances.
It's unclear what behavior the user should expect when related models are passed
`None`
data.
It's unclear how the user should expect to-many relationships to handle updates, creations and deletions of multiple records.

Using the
`depth`
option on
`ModelSerializer`
will now create
read-only nested serializers
by default.

and/or
`update()`

120|SERIALIZER|The **SERIALIZER** is the fundamental base class within the REST framework used for the serialization and deserialization of data, serving as a technical bridge that converts complex data types—such as querysets and model instances—to native Python datatypes and JSON, and vice versa. Functioning similarly to a Django form, the **SERIALIZER** provides a standard API for data representation, validation, and persistence, offering an explicit alternative to the `ModelSerializer` when automatic field generation is insufficient or not required.

Technically, the **SERIALIZER** manages data through attributes like `_declared_fields` and a `data` property, and it is capable of handling both single instances and lists of objects via the `many=True` flag. It implements a robust validation and transformation pipeline featuring methods such as `is_valid()`, `validate()`, and field-level validation via `.validate_<field_name>` methods, while also utilizing validator components that can receive the **SERIALIZER** instance as context if `requires_context` is enabled. For data persistence, it provides `save()`, `create()`, and `update()` methods, and it now includes `set_value` as a method.

Furthermore, the **SERIALIZER** can act as a `Field` itself to enable nested representations of complex objects and relationships. To ensure operational stability, it should not raise `PermissionDenied` during list actions to guarantee the return of the entire dataset. # Django REST framework 3.0¶ {#django-rest-framework-30}

The 3.0 release of Django REST framework is the result of almost four years of iteration and refinement. It comprehensively addresses some of the previous remaining design issues in serializers, fields and the generic views.

This release is incremental in nature. There
are
some breaking API changes, and upgrading
will
require you to read the release notes carefully, but the migration path should otherwise be relatively straightforward.

The difference in quality of the REST framework API and implementation should make writing, maintaining and debugging your application far easier.

 are vastly easier to understand and debug, and that make it easy to switch between the implicit
`ModelSerializer`
class and the explicit
`Serializer`
class.
A new
`BaseSerializer`
class, making it easier to write serializers for alternative storage backends, or to completely customize your serialization and validation logic.
A cleaner fields API including new classes such as
`ListField`
and
`MultipleChoiceField`
.
Super simple default implementations (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/blob/main/rest_framework/mixins.py)
for the generic views.
Support for overriding how validation errors are handled by your API.
A metadata API that allows you to customize how
`OPTIONS`
requests are handled by your API.
A more compact
64| JSON output with unicode style encoding turned on by default.
Templated based HTML form rendering for serializers. This will be finalized as public API in the upcoming 3.1 release.

Significant new functionality continues to be planned for the 3.1 and 3.2 releases. These releases will correspond to the two
Kickstarter stretch goals (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/tomchristie/django-rest-framework-3)
- "Feature improvements" and "Admin interface". Further 3.x releases will present simple upgrades, without the same level of fundamental API changes necessary for the 3.0 release.

#### REST framework: Under the hood.¶ {#rest-framework-under-the-hood}

This talk from the
Django: Under the Hood (https://www.djangounderthehood.com/)
event in Amsterdam, Nov 2014, gives some good background context on the design decisions behind 3.0.

Below is an in-depth guide to the API changes and migration notes for 3.0.

## Request objects¶ {#request-objects}

#### The.dataand.query_paramsproperties.¶ {#the-data-and-query_params-properties}

The usage of
`request.DATA`
and
`request.FILES`
is now pending deprecation in favor of a single
`request.data`
attribute that contains
all
the parsed data.

Having separate attributes is reasonable for web applications that only ever parse url-encoded or multipart requests, but makes less sense for the
64| general-purpose request parsing that REST framework supports.

## Serializers¶ {#serializers}

#### Single-step object creation.¶ {#single-step-object-creation}

Previously the serializers used a two-step object creation, as follows:

Validating the data would create an object instance. This instance would be available as
`serializer.object`
.
Calling
`serializer.save()`
would then save the object instance to the database.

This style is in-line with how the
`ModelForm`
class works in Django, but is problematic for a number of reasons:

Some data, such as many-to-many relationships, cannot be added to the object instance until after it has been saved. This type of data needed to be hidden in some undocumented state on the object instance, or kept as state on the serializer instance so that it could be used when
`.save()`
is called.
Instantiating model instances directly means that you cannot use model manager classes for instance creation, e.g.
`ExampleModel.objects.create(...)`
. Manager classes are an excellent layer at which to enforce business logic and
64|, like so:

Validating the data makes the cleaned data available as
`serializer.validated_data`
.
Calling
`serializer.save()`
then saves and returns the new object instance.

The resulting API changes are further detailed below.

#### Usingserializers.ValidationError.¶ {#using-serializersvalidationerror}

Previously
`serializers.ValidationError`

`django.core.exceptions.ValidationError`

`APIException`

The reason behind this is that Django's

65| that whenever raising validation errors you should prefer using the

#### Writable nested serialization.¶ {#writable-nested-serialization}

REST framework 2.x attempted to automatically support writable nested serialization, but the behavior was complex and non-obvious. Attempting to automatically handle these case is problematic:

There can be complex dependencies involved in order of saving multiple related model instances.
It's unclear what behavior the user should expect when related models are passed
`None`
data.
It's unclear how the user should expect to-many relationships to handle updates, creations and deletions of multiple records.

`depth`

reference: Override perform_create (and perform_update): it's the save hook for implicit request data, and you can raise a ValidationError inside it to validate at the point of database save — that error flows through DRF's handling to a 400.
reference_contexts: These hooks are particularly useful for setting attributes that are implicit in the request, but are not part of the request data.

This can be useful if you need some validation logic to apply at the point of database save.

Signature: ValidationError(detail=None, code=None) The ValidationError exception is slightly different from the other APIException classes: The detail argument may be a list or dictionary of error details, and may also be a nested data structure.
llm_response:
To inject the current user and perform extra validation right before the database write in a generic view, you should use the **`perform_create`** hook (for new objects) or the **`perform_update`** hook (for existing objects).

### How to implement
You can override these methods in your view to inject the user via the `serializer.save()` method and perform custom validation logic before that call.

**Example for `perform_create`:**
```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    # Perform custom validation
    queryset = SignupRequest.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)
    if queryset.exists():
        raise serializers.ValidationError('You have already signed up')
    
    # Inject the user and save
    serializer.save(user=self.request.user)
```

### Behavior of `ValidationError`
When you raise a `ValidationError` within these hooks:
*   **Exception Handling:** The REST framework automatically catches the `ValidationError`.
*   **Response:** It triggers the framework's default exception handler to return an **HTTP 400 Bad Request** response to the client.
*   **Usage:** You should raise `serializers.ValidationError` (using the namespaced `import serializers` style) rather than Django's built-in `ValidationError` to ensure compatibility with the API's error handling and formatting.

#### Customizing error responses.¶ {#customizing-error-responses}

The generic views now raise

This change means that you can now easily customize the style of error responses across your entire API, without having to modify any of the generic views.

## The metadata API¶ {#the-metadata-api}

Behavior for dealing with
`OPTIONS`
requests was previously built directly into the class-based views. This has now been properly separated out into a Metadata API that allows the same pluggable style as other API policies in REST framework.

This makes it far easier to use a different style for
`OPTIONS`
responses throughout your API, and makes it possible to create third-party metadata policies.

## Serializers as HTML forms¶ {#serializers-as-html-forms}

REST framework 3.0 includes templated HTML form rendering for serializers.

This API should not yet be considered finalized, and will only be

promoted to public API for the 3.1 release.

Significant changes that you do need to be aware of include:

Nested HTML forms are now supported, for example, a
`UserSerializer`
with a nested
`ProfileSerializer`
will now render a nested
`fieldset`
when used in the browsable API.
Nested lists of HTML forms are not yet supported, but are planned for 3.1.
Because we now use templated HTML form generation,
the
`widget`
option is no longer available for serializer fields
. You can instead control the template that is used for a given field, by using the
`style`
dictionary.

llm_response:
When using a `HyperlinkedModelSerializer` with a custom `lookup_field`, you must ensure that both the API views and the serializer classes set the lookup fields to match.

Specifically, you must ensure the following:

*   **View Configuration:** The view must set the `lookup_field` attribute to the model field used for performing object lookups.
*   **Serializer Configuration:** The serializer must define the same `lookup_field` for its hyperlinked fields. This can be done in two ways:
    *   **Using `extra_kwargs`:** You can configure the `lookup_field` within the `extra_kwargs` setting in the serializer's `Meta` class.
    *   **Explicit Field Declaration:** You can explicitly declare the field (e.g., `url = serializers.HyperlinkedIdentityField(...)`) and provide the `lookup_field` argument directly to that field.

The documentation notes that matching these configurations can be "fiddly," and recommends printing the `repr` of the `HyperlinkedModelSerializer` instance to inspect exactly which view names and lookup fields the relationships are expected to map to.

## Hyperlinking our API¶ {#hyperlinking-our-api}

Dealing with relationships between entities is one of the more challenging aspects of Web API design.  There are a number of different ways that we might choose to represent a relationship:

Using primary keys.
Using hyperlinking between entities.
Using a unique identifying slug field on the related entity.
Using the default string representation of the related entity.
Nesting the related entity inside the parent representation.
Some other custom representation.

REST framework supports all of these styles, and can

apply them across forward or reverse relationships, or apply them across custom managers such as generic foreign keys.

Relationships use

## HyperlinkedModelSerializer¶ {#hyperlinkedmodelserializer}

The
`HyperlinkedModelSerializer`
class is similar to the
`ModelSerializer`
class except that it uses hyperlinks to represent relationships, rather than primary keys.

By default the serializer will include a
`url`
field instead of a primary key field.

The url field will be represented using a
`HyperlinkedIdentityField`
serializer field, and any relationships on the model will be represented using a
`HyperlinkedRelatedField`
serializer field.

You can explicitly include the primary key by adding it to the
`fields`
option, for example:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','id','account_name','users','created']`


### Absolute and relative URLs¶ {#absolute-and-relative-urls}

When instantiating a
`HyperlinkedModelSerializer`
you must include the current
`request`
in the serializer context, for example:


`serializer=AccountSerializer(queryset,context={'request':request})`


Doing so will ensure that the hyperlinks can include an appropriate hostname,
so that the resulting representation uses fully qualified URLs, such as:


`http://api.example.com/accounts/1/`


Rather than relative URLs, such as:


`/accounts/1/`

There needs to be a way of determining which views should be used for hyperlinking to model instances.

By default hyperlinks are expected to correspond to a view name that matches the style

`pk`

'}}`

Using primary keys.
Using hyperlinking between entities.
Using a unique identifying slug field on the related entity.
Using the default string representation of the related entity.
Nesting the related entity inside the parent representation.
Some other custom representation.

user_input: Our album list endpoint went from 40ms to about four seconds after I changed the tracks field to render the full nested track objects instead of just their ids. Someone told me to add select_related('tracks') to the queryset and the ORM threw an error at me instead. Why doesn't the framework deal with this itself, and how do I tell which optimisation goes with which field?
reference: The framework deliberately doesn't optimise the queryset for you — it makes no attempt to infer select_related / prefetch_related from your serializer, because that would be too much magic. Any field that spans an ORM relation, whether it's a declared relational field or a plain field reaching across a relation via `source`, can cost an extra query per object, and with many=True over a large queryset that becomes the N+1 you're seeing. Fixing it is your job, and which tool applies is decided by the relation, not by the serializer: select_related resolves forward single-valued relations (ForeignKey, OneToOne) with a SQL join, while a reverse or multi-valued relation like `tracks` cannot be joined that way and has to use prefetch_related — which is exactly why select_related('tracks') errored. Pass the optimised queryset to the serializer (Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks')) and the extra hits disappear.
reference_contexts: REST Framework does not attempt to automatically optimize querysets passed to serializers in terms of select_related and prefetch_related since it would be too much magic. A serializer with a field spanning an ORM relation through its source attribute could require an additional database hit to fetch related objects from the database. It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid additional database hits which could occur while using a serializer.
If AlbumSerializer is used to serialize a fairly large queryset with many=True then it could be a serious performance problem.
qs = Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks') # No additional database hits required print(AlbumSerializer(qs, many=True).data)
llm_response:
The framework does not automatically optimize querysets because it would be "too much magic." It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid the N+1 problem that occurs when a serializer field spans an ORM relation.

To determine which optimization to use, follow these rules based on the type of relationship:

*   **For `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` relationships:** Use `select_related()` to fetch related objects in the same SQL query.
*   **For reverse and many-to-many relationships:** Use `prefetch_related()` to load collections of related objects in a separate batch.

You should apply these optimizations to the queryset in your view, typically by overriding the `get_queryset()` method. For example:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    # Use select_related for ForeignKey/OneToOneField
    # Use prefetch_related for reverse/many-to-many relationships
    return Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks')
```

If you are seeing an error when using `select_related('tracks')`, it is likely because `tracks` is a reverse relationship (a one-to-many relationship from `Album` to `Track`), which requires `prefetch_related()` instead of `select_related()`.

## Adding login to the Browsable API¶ {#adding-login-to-the-browsable-api}

If you open a browser and navigate to the browsable API at the moment, you'll find that you're no longer able to create new code snippets.  In order to do so we'd need to be able to login as a user.

We can add a login view for use with the browsable API, by editing the URLconf in our project-level
`urls.py`
file.

Add the following import at the top of the file:


`fromdjango.urlsimportpath,include`


And, at the end of the file, add a pattern to include the login and logout views for the browsable API.


`urlpatterns+=[path("api-auth/",include("rest_framework.urls")),]`


The
`'api-auth/'`
part of pattern can actually be whatever URL you want to use.

Now if you open up the browser again and refresh the page you'll see a 'Login' link in

the top right of the page.  If you log in as one of the users you created earlier, you'll be able to create code snippets again.

Once you've created a few code snippets, navigate to the '/users/' endpoint, and notice that the representation includes a list of the snippet ids that are associated with each user, in each user's 'snippets' field.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

Really we'd like all code snippets to be visible to anyone, but also make sure that only the user that created a code snippet is able to update or delete it.

To do that we're going to need to create a custom permission.

In the snippets app, create a new file,
`permissions.py`

Now we can add that custom permission to our snippet instance endpoint, by editing the
`permission_classes`
property on the
`SnippetDetail`
view class:


`permission_classes=[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly,IsOwnerOrReadOnly]`


Make sure to also import the
`

IsOwnerOrReadOnly`
class.


`fromsnippets.permissionsimportIsOwnerOrReadOnly`


Now, if you open a browser again, you find that the 'DELETE' and 'PUT' actions only appear on a snippet instance endpoint if you're logged in as the same user that created the code snippet.

## Authenticating with the API¶ {#authenticating-with-the-api}

Because we now have a set of permissions on the API, we need to authenticate our requests to it if we want to edit any snippets.  We haven't set up any
authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)

`SessionAuthentication`

Save and deletion hooks

The following methods are provided by the mixin classes, and provide easy overriding of the object save or deletion behavior.

`perform_create(self, serializer)`
- Called by
`CreateModelMixin`
when saving a new object instance.
`perform_update(self, serializer)`
- Called by
`UpdateModelMixin`
when saving an existing object instance.
`perform_destroy(self, instance)`
- Called by
`DestroyModelMixin`
when deleting an object instance.

These hooks are particularly useful for setting attributes that are implicit in the request, but are not part of the request data.  For instance, you might set an attribute on the object based on the request user, or based on a URL keyword argument.


`defperform_create(self,serializer):serializer.save(user=self.request.user)`


These override points are also particularly useful for adding behavior that occurs before or after saving an object, such

as emailing a confirmation, or logging the update.


`defperform_update(self,serializer):instance=serializer.save()send_email_confirmation(user=self.request.user,modified=instance)`


You can also use these hooks to provide additional validation, by raising a
`ValidationError()`
. This can be useful if you need some validation logic to apply at the point of database save. For example:


`defperform_create(self,serializer):queryset=SignupRequest.objects.filter(user=self.request.user)ifqueryset.exists():raiseValidationError('You have already signed up')serializer.save(user=self.request.user)`

## Adding login to the Browsable API¶ {#adding-login-to-the-browsable-api}

If you open a browser and navigate to the browsable API at the moment, you'll find that you're no longer able to create new code snippets.  In order to do so we'd need to be able to login as a user.

We can add a login view for use with the browsable API, by editing the URLconf in our project-level
`urls.py`
file.

Add the following import at the top of the file:


`fromdjango.urlsimportpath,include`


And, at the end of the file, add a pattern to include the login and logout views for the browsable API.


`urlpatterns+=[path("api-auth/",include("rest_framework.urls")),]`


The
`'api-auth/'`
part of pattern can actually be whatever URL you want to use.

Now if you open up the browser again and refresh the page you'll see a 'Login' link in
35| the top right of the page.  If you log in as one of the users you created earlier, you'll be able to create code snippets again.

Once you've created a few code snippets, navigate to the '/users/' endpoint, and notice that the representation includes a list of the snippet ids that are associated with each user, in each user's 'snippets' field.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

Really we'd like all code snippets to be visible to anyone, but also make sure that only the user that created a code snippet is able to update or delete it.

To do that we're going to need to create a custom permission.

In the snippets app, create a new file,
`permissions.py`

llm_response:
To automatically generate an authentication token for every user at account creation and backfill tokens for existing users, you can use the following patterns:

### 1. Automatic Token Creation at Account Creation
You can catch the `post_save` signal for the `User` model to automatically generate a token whenever a new user instance is saved. Place this code in an installed `models.py` module or another location imported by Django on startup:

```python
from django.conf import settings
from django.db.models.signals import post_save
from django.dispatch import receiver
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

@receiver(post_save, sender=settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL)
def create_auth_token(sender, instance=None, created=False, **kwargs):
    if created:
        Token.objects.create(user=instance)
```

### 2. Backfilling Tokens for Existing Users
To generate tokens for users that were created before the signal was implemented, you can run the following logic:

```python
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

for user in User.objects.all():
    Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user)
```

**Requirements:**
*   Ensure `rest_framework.authtoken` is included in your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting.
*   Run `manage.py migrate` after adding the application to your settings to create the necessary database tables.

### BasicAuthentication¶ {#basicauthentication}

This authentication scheme uses
HTTP Basic Authentication (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2617)
, signed against a user's username and password.  Basic authentication is generally only appropriate for testing.

If successfully authenticated,
`BasicAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be
`None`
.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:


`WWW-Authenticate:Basicrealm="api"`

### TokenAuthentication¶ {#

tokenauthentication}

Note
The token authentication provided by Django REST framework is a fairly simple implementation.
For an implementation which allows more than one token per user, has some tighter security implementation details, and supports token expiry, please see the
Django REST Knox (https://github.com/James1345/django-rest-knox)
third party package.

This authentication scheme uses a simple token-based HTTP Authentication scheme.  Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.

To use the
`TokenAuthentication`
scheme you'll need to
configure the authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/#setting-the-authentication-scheme)
to include
`TokenAuthentication`
, and additionally include
`rest_framework.authtoken`
in your
`INSTALLED_APPS`
setting:


`INSTALLED_APPS=[...'rest_framework.authtoken']`


Make sure to run
`manage.py migrate`
after changing your settings.

The
`rest_framework.authtoken`
app provides Django database migrations.

You'll also need to create tokens for your users.


`fromrest_framework.authtoken.modelsimportTokentoken=Token.objects.create(user=...)print(token.key)`


For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the
`Authorization`
HTTP header.  The key should be prefixed by the string literal "Token", with whitespace separating the two strings.  For example:


`Authorization:Token9944b09199c

62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`


If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as
`Bearer`
, simply subclass
`TokenAuthentication`
and set the
`keyword`
class variable.

If successfully authenticated,
`TokenAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be a
`rest_framework.authtoken.models.Token`
instance.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:


`WWW-Authenticate:Token`

user_input: How does DRF's Request relate to the parsers, and what does request.data give me that request.POST doesn't?
reference: request.data is DRF's flexible replacement for request.POST: it handles arbitrary parsed content for POST, PUT and PATCH, not just form data. The parser classes DRF selects do the actual parsing, so request.data works across formats like JSON.
reference_contexts: The core functionality of the Request object is the request.data attribute, which is similar to request.POST , but more useful for working with Web APIs.
request.data can handle incoming json requests, but it can also handle other formats.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning 405 Method Not Allowed responses when appropriate, and handling any ParseError exceptions that occur when accessing request.data with malformed input.
request.data will be populated with a dictionary of data.
request.query_params is a more correctly named synonym for request.GET .
llm_response:
DRF's `Request` object relates to parsers through the `request.data` property. When `request.data` is accessed, the REST framework examines the `Content-Type` header of the incoming request to determine which parser to use. The view's `parser_classes` or the global `DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES` setting define the list of available `Parser` instances that the framework uses to populate `request.data`.

`request.data` provides several advantages over `request.POST`:

*   **Flexible Media Types:** Unlike `request.POST`, which is designed specifically for form data, `request.data` supports REST framework's flexible parsing, allowing you to handle various media types such as JSON.
*   **Method Support:** `request.data` supports parsing the content of HTTP methods other than `POST`, including `PUT` and `PATCH` requests.
*   **Consolidated Data:** `request.data` includes all parsed content, covering both file and non-file inputs, whereas `request.POST` only handles form data and does not include items from `request.FILES`.

## Authentication¶ {#authentication}

REST framework provides flexible, per-request authentication, that gives you the ability to:

Support the use of multiple authentication policies.
Provide both user and token information associated with the incoming request.

Yes, the `DefaultRouter` class automatically creates an API root view for you, which makes your manual `api_root` function redundant and allows you to delete it.

### How registrations map to URLs
When you register a ViewSet with a router using the `register()` method, the router automatically generates URL patterns and names based on the provided `prefix` and the ViewSet's actions.

*   **URL Patterns:** The router maps the `prefix` to standard CRUD actions. For example, registering a ViewSet with the prefix `r'users'` generates:
    *   `^users/$` (mapped to the `list` action)
    *   `^users/{pk}/$` (mapped to the `retrieve` action)
*   **URL Names:** The names are generated using the `basename` argument. If you do not provide a `basename`, it is automatically determined from the `queryset` attribute of the ViewSet. The naming convention follows the pattern `{basename}-list` and `{basename}-detail`.
*   **Extra Actions:** If you use the `@action` decorator on methods within your ViewSet, the router generates additional routes. By default, the URL pattern is based on the method name, and the URL name is the combination of the `basename` and the hyphenated method name (e.g., `{basename}-{method_name}`). You can override these defaults by providing `url_path` and `url_name` arguments to the `@action` decorator.

**Note:** When registering ViewSets, do not include a trailing slash in the prefix (e.g., use `r'users'`, not `r'users/'`). The router handles trailing slashes automatically based on your configuration.

Additionally, it supports API versioning through the `versioning_class` attribute and handles CSRF validation internally while initializing the request object.

From a schema and documentation perspective, APIVIEW is identified by the SchemaGenerator to compile the API schema, though it possesses certain limitations when used with AutoSchema; specifically, for basic subclasses, default schema introspection is limited to URL kwarg path parameters. Notably, the `exclude_from_schema` attribute has been deprecated in favor of setting `schema = None`. 

In practical implementation, APIVIEW is used to create custom views (such as ProfileList and ProfileDetail) and is inherited by specific views like ContactListView, ContactDetailView, and UploadView. It is the standard location where `APIException` and other handled exceptions are raised. Finally, unlike some higher-level abstractions in the framework, when using APIVIEW, pagination must be invoked manually via the pagination API.|39

Resource routing allows you to quickly declare all of the common routes for a given resourceful controller.  Instead of declaring separate routes for your index... a resourceful route declares them in a single line of code.

# Routers¶ {#routers}

Resource routing allows you to quickly declare all of the common routes for a given resourceful controller.  Instead of declaring separate routes for your index... a resourceful route declares them in a single line of code.
—
Ruby on Rails Documentation (https://guides.rubyonrails.org/routing.html)

Some Web frameworks such as Rails provide functionality for automatically determining how the URLs for an application should be mapped to the logic that deals with handling incoming requests.

REST framework adds support for automatic URL routing to Django, and provides you with a simple, quick and consistent way of wiring your view logic to a set of URLs.

## Usage¶ {#usage}

Here's an example of a simple URL conf, that uses
`SimpleRouter`
.


`fromrest_frameworkimportrouters

`register()`
method:

`prefix`
- The URL prefix to use for this set of routes.
`viewset`
- The viewset class.

Optionally, you may also specify an additional argument:

`basename`
- The base to use for the URL names that are created.  If unset the basename will be automatically generated based on the

llm_response:
The format of the response is determined by the **content negotiation** process, which selects a renderer based on the incoming request's `Accept` header and the priority of the renderers configured for the view.

### What decides the format
*   **Content Negotiation:** The `DEFAULT_CONTENT_NEGOTIATION_CLASS` (defaulting to `DefaultContentNegotiation`) determines how a renderer is selected. It evaluates the client's `Accept` header against the available renderers.
*   **Renderer Priority:** If a client does not specify an `Accept` header or sends `Accept: */*`, the framework selects the first renderer listed in the view's `renderer_classes` or the global `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES` setting.
*   **Browsable API:** The `BrowsableAPIRenderer` is designed to provide a web-based HTML interface. When a web browser makes a request, the API often defaults to returning an HTML-formatted representation.

### Why you and the front-end team see different formats
The difference in output format is likely due to the `Accept` headers sent by your respective clients:
*   **Your client:** Likely sends an `Accept: application/json` header or is configured to prioritize `JSONRenderer`.
*   **Front-end team:** If they are accessing the endpoint via a web browser, the browser typically sends an `Accept` header that prioritizes HTML, causing the framework to select `BrowsableAPIRenderer` (or another HTML-based renderer) instead of `JSONRenderer`.

### How to control the format
1.  **Global/View Configuration:** You can control the available renderers using the `renderer_classes` attribute on a view or the `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES` setting.
2.  **Forcing a format:** You can override the default content negotiation behavior by using the `format` query parameter (e.g., `?format=json`), provided `URL_FORMAT_OVERRIDE` is enabled.
3.  **Customizing Browsable API:** If you want to change how the browsable API behaves, you can subclass `BrowsableAPIRenderer` and override the `get_default_renderer()` method to force a specific renderer (like `JSONRenderer`) even when the browsable API is used.

## Self describing APIs¶ {#self-describing-apis}

The browsable API that REST framework provides makes it possible for your API to be entirely self describing.  The documentation for each API endpoint can be provided simply by visiting the URL in your browser

The title that is used in the browsable API is generated from the view class name or function name.  Any trailing

When working with viewsets, an appropriate suffix is appended to each generated view.  For example, the view set
`UserViewSet`

`User List`
and
`User Instance`
.

.

REST framework APIs also support programmatically accessible descriptions, using the
`OPTIONS`
HTTP method.  A view will respond to an
`OPTIONS`

When using the generic views, any
